Backyard play turf for Union Park families

Playground turf in Union Park runs $10–$25 a square foot installed, typically $12–$19, with the shock pad sized to whatever equipment sits on top of it. About half of Union Park's roughly 10,450 residents identify as Hispanic or Latino in the 2020 Census, and this is one of the more family-heavy communities we work in, which is exactly the mix that keeps backyard play turf on our schedule here.

Reviewed by Luis Austin, owner · Last reviewed September 21, 2026

A backyard play area near Jay Blanchard Park

Say a Union Park family a few blocks from Jay Blanchard Park wants a 300 sq ft play area for a swing set and a trampoline, on a lot where the rest of the backyard stays open lawn. At $10–$25 a square foot installed, that runs roughly $3,000 to $7,500, with most jobs closer to $12–$19 a foot, or about $3,600 to $5,700. Shock-pad thickness under the swing set's fall zone accounts for most of the spread within that range, since a taller structure needs a deeper pad than a low trampoline does. The rest of the yard, turfed separately in ordinary silica-infill turf, prices at the standard residential range rather than the play-area rate.

Why families here often build rather than drive to the park

Jay Blanchard Park, off Dean Road, and the paved Little Econ Greenway running through it are Union Park's main public green space, and both see heavy use on weekends. A backyard play surface doesn't replace a public trail or a ball field, but it does cover the smaller, everyday need, a swing set, a trampoline, a spot for a toddler to fall safely, without loading kids into a car first. Material safety for a play surface is worth reading alongside this page.

Why the turf, pad, and equipment all answer to their own spec sheet

A Union Park play area is really three separate products, turf, shock pad, and the equipment itself, each installed to its own manufacturer's specifications, and mixing components without checking that they were tested together can leave a system that looks correct on paper without the coverage a matched combination provides. A pad rated for a certain fall height under one turf backing isn't automatically rated the same way under a different backing's thickness or drainage profile. Asking whether the specific pad, turf, and equipment combination going into a project has documented test data together, not just each piece individually, is worth confirming before installation.

The infill rule that actually governs a Union Park play area

Florida's May 2026 turf standard allows rubber or other synthetic infill only inside the footprint of playground equipment itself, never across the rest of a residential lawn. In practice that means a Union Park backyard often carries two different builds side by side: a rubber or engineered infill zone sized to the equipment's fall height directly under a swing set or slide, and ordinary silica-infilled turf everywhere else in the yard. the exact rule wording is on our HB 683 page.

Keeping the sand under a play area able to drain

The state's turf rule bars compacting the subgrade under any synthetic surface, including a Union Park playground system, so tightly that it stops the native sand from percolating water down and away. A play area's base gets built firm enough to support a shock pad and repeated impact from jumping and landing, but that firmness has to stop short of sealing off the sand beneath it. A base that's been over-compacted in the name of stability ends up trapping water at the surface instead, which is exactly the outcome the rule is written to prevent.

Low-E glass facing a play area

Checking for low-emissivity glass near a Union Park play area deserves the same attention as checking it anywhere else on a property with turf: a patio door or window built with that coating can throw back enough concentrated sunlight to soften polyethylene fiber, which begins to give around 175 to 200°F, a lower bar than most homeowners assume a mere reflection could reach. A scorched spot on equipment that otherwise sits in regular shade is the usual giveaway that this is happening rather than ordinary wear. Shifting the equipment's position or the play area's layout by a few feet typically resolves it without touching the turf or pad specification at all.

The final walk-through before handing off a play surface

The last step on a Union Park playground project is infilling at the manufacturer's specified rate, then walking the finished surface to check for flat, even coverage and confirm nothing shifted during the last stages of the build. This walk-through is where a crew catches a low spot, an uneven seam, or a containment edge that needs a final adjustment before calling the job finished. Skipping this check and assuming a play surface is ready just because the visible steps are done is how small problems make it to the first day of use instead of getting caught beforehand.

What a two-year check on a play area actually looks for

By the two-year mark, a Union Park play area has been through two rainy seasons, enough time to reveal whether infill has started drifting toward or past the containment edge and whether seams that looked flat on day one still do after repeated impact and weather. This earlier check is different from a pad's longer-term fall-height recheck years down the road; it's mainly about confirming the surface is still performing the way it did at installation rather than judging whether the pad itself has aged out of its original rating. Catching drifted infill or a lifting seam at two years keeps either fix small.

Building a play area over Union Park's flatwoods sand

The same Immokalee and Myakka fine sands that sit under most Union Park lawns also sit under a backyard play area, and a seasonally high water table means the base has to work harder here than it would on a better-draining ridge lot elsewhere in Central Florida. We build toward the deeper end of the state's crushed-rock range under a play zone specifically, since standing water under a shock pad defeats the point of the pad faster than under open lawn.

Questions people ask

Can rubber infill go anywhere in a Union Park backyard?

Only inside the footprint of playground equipment, under Florida's May 2026 turf rule. The rest of the yard has to use silica sand, rock, shell or a coated natural-material infill instead.

Does Jay Blanchard Park count toward what a Union Park yard needs?

No, a public park doesn't change any permitting or setback rule for a private backyard project. It's simply the community's main open space, which is part of why backyard play turf tends to serve as a supplement rather than a replacement here.
